en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhūtagāma-vagga 11.
The Training Rule on Plants.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work, were cutting down trees and having them cut down.
One certain monk of Āḷavī was cutting down a tree.
The deity dwelling in that tree said this to that monk:
“Venerable sir, do not cut down my dwelling while you intend to build one for yourself!
But that bhikkhu, disregarding her, continued cutting; he even struck the arm of that deity’s child.
Then it occurred to that deity:
“What if I were to deprive this bhikkhu of life right here?
Then it occurred to that deity:
“It would not be fitting for me to deprive this bhikkhu of life right here.”
“What if I were to report this matter to the Blessed One?
Then that deity approached the Blessed One; having approached, she reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Excellent, excellent, deity!”
"It is well that you, goddess, did not deprive that bhikkhu of life.
Had you, goddess, deprived that bhikkhu of life today, you would have produced much demerit.
Go, goddess, to a certain place where there is a secluded tree; approach it."
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, cut down trees and have them cut down? These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, are harming a living being with a single sense-faculty!
The bhikkhus heard those people complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the bhikkhus of Āḷavī cut down trees themselves or have them cut down? … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that you cut down trees yourselves or have them cut down?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, cut down trees yourselves or have them cut down by others?”
"For people, O foolish men, perceive a living being in a tree.
This, O foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘Whatever monk should intentionally cut off the green foliage of a tree, there is an offense of wrong-doing.’"
“Destruction of vegetation is an offense entailing expiation.
Here, “vegetation” means the five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and fifthly, seed-seeds.
Root-seed means:
turmeric, ginger, *vacā*, *vacatta*, *ativisa*, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *usīra*, *bhaddamuttaka*, or whatever other [plants] there are that grow from roots, are produced from roots—this is called root-seed.
Stem-seed means:
The *assattha*, *nigrodha*, *pilakkha*, *udumbara*, *kacchaka*, *kapitthana*, and whatever other plants there are that grow from a trunk, are produced from a trunk—this is called "trunk-seed.
As for "joint-seed":
sugar cane, bamboo, reeds, and whatever other plants there are that grow from a joint, are produced from a joint—this is called "joint-seed."
"Tip-top seed" means:
the *ajjuka*, the *phaṇijjaka*, the *hirivera*, or whatever other plants there are that grow from the tip, are produced from the tip; this is called "tip-top seed.
"Seed-of-seed" means:
Grain for the morning meal, grain for the evening meal, or whatever else there is that grows from seed, is produced from seed—this is called "seed-seed.
If one, perceiving it as seed, cuts it or causes it to be cut, breaks it or causes it to be broken, cooks it or causes it to be cooked, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one, being doubtful about whether it is seed, cuts it or causes it to be cut, breaks it or causes it to be broken, cooks it or causes it to be cooked, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one cuts, or causes to be cut, breaks, or causes to be broken, cooks, or causes to be cooked, while perceiving what is seedless as having seeds, there is no offense.
If one perceives what is seedless as having seeds, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one is in doubt regarding what is seedless, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is seedless and he perceives it as seedless, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he says: "Know this; give this; bring this; there is need for this; make this allowable."
Unintentionally,
through lack of mindfulness,
or not knowing.
[This applies] to one who is insane,
and to the first offender.
The first training rule on plants is finished.
